headline: Peanut Bunker Pours Through the Shoal — Bass and Blues Feed Below
subhead: Bunker rafts are pushing hard through the Stratford Shoal narrows, and the bass and blues stacked underneath are the best story in the Central Sound right now.
body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning parked off the Shoal doing nothing but watching bait, and it was worth the gas. Peanut bunker are pouring through the Stratford Shoal narrows in tight, nervous rafts — not the loose scattered pods you see in July, but dense schools getting squeezed by the current the way this stretch of Sound always squeezes bait when it narrows between the Connecticut shore and Long Island. Terns were working them hard by 7 AM, diving in short, aggressive drops instead of the lazy circling you see when there's nothing pushing from below. That's the tell. When the birds go from circling to diving, something's under the bait, and Tuesday it was bass and blues both.

The blitz activity at the Shoal has been real, not a one-off. I've had reports of the same thing off Charles Island and along the western edge of the Norwalk Islands — bunker schools getting pinned against rock piles and current lines, stripers and blues working them from underneath in bursts that last twenty minutes then go quiet before firing again a quarter mile down current. This kind of visible surface blitzing in mid-August is a little unusual for this zone — usually by now the bait's thinned out and the fish have gone deep and lazy. What we're seeing instead looks like early staging behavior, fish grouping up on bait ahead of the fall push south, and the timing lines up with the tide.

We're two days off the new moon, and the tidal flow built into that cycle has been sharpening the bite at every piece of current-driven structure in the zone — we said that would happen back on the 7th, and the Shoal rip is proving it out. Bigger water movement means bait gets funneled harder through the pinch points — Stratford Shoal, the cut between the Norwalk Islands, the rip off Middle Ground Light — and the fish know exactly where to sit and wait. My best window has been the last two hours of the outgoing, when bait gets swept off the flats and concentrated right on the edge of the rip. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked with a slow lift-and-drop through the frothy water, have been drawing bass in the 24 to 32-inch range with the occasional overslot mixed in. Blues in the 3 to 6-pound class are riding the same bait and will absolutely destroy a metal — a Deadly Dowsing or a Kastmaster thrown into the boil and ripped back fast is about as close to a guaranteed hookup as this sport gets right now.

We also called the bluefish resurgence spreading east from the Western Sound's reef structure, and that's exactly the pattern playing out — the blues have shown up in real numbers off the Norwalk Islands and are pushing east toward Charles Island and the Shoal. Porgy fishing has held up as the more dependable, less dramatic bite underneath all this — bloodworms and clam belly on high-low rigs in 20 to 30 feet of water over the reef structure off Port Jeff and the Norwalk rock piles are producing steady catches of decent-sized scup, the kind of bite you can set your watch to even on days the blitz doesn't show.

Fluke have been the quiet disappointment. Drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails through the deeper cuts off Middle Ground and the mouth of Port Jeff Harbor has produced fish, but they've been mostly short, with only the occasional keeper in the 19 to 21-inch range mixed in. The water there is warm and stable — Kings Point is reading 70.9 and New London's holding at 69.4, so there's a real west-to-east gradient across this stretch, and the fluke seem to be sitting in whatever cooler pockets they can find rather than feeding hard. I'd call fluke a secondary target this week, not a primary trip.

Weakfish have been a pleasant surprise mixed into the bass and blue action at dusk around the Shoal and off Charles Island — nothing like the numbers from twenty years ago, but legal fish in the 16 to 20-inch class have come on diamond jigs tipped with squid strips worked slow along the bottom edge of the rip on the last of the incoming.

Looking ahead, the tide keeps building through the week, and if the bait holds its position at the Shoal and around the Norwalk Islands, I'd expect the blitz pattern to continue, maybe intensify, especially on the outgoing around Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground. The risk is wind — if we get a stretch of southwest blow it'll scatter these bunker schools and spread the fish out, which would turn this from a targeted bite back into a search-and-hope situation. I haven't heard of any bonito or albie sightings pushing into the Central Sound yet, but with bait this dense and water this warm, I'll be watching the rips closely over the next week. If I had one trip to make, I'd be at the Shoal on the last two hours of the outgoing with a bucktail rod ready and a metal rod on deck, because right now that's where the bait is, and the bait is telling the whole story.
